notes.meaning: Samson went to Gaza, a strong Philistine city deep in enemy land. There he saw a prostitute and slept with her. Matthew Henry notes that his sin began with his eyes. Unlike an earlier story, the text does not say this came from the Lord. Some old translations call the woman an innkeeper, and she may have been both.

differ.view: Some say the words 'went in' do not have to mean sex. Staying at a prostitute's house may have been a way to enter the town without being noticed, like the spies at Rahab's house. This view admits most readers take it as sex.

notes.meaning: The people of Gaza heard Samson was there. They set guards at the city gate and waited quietly. They felt so sure of catching him that they planned to kill him in the morning, and they probably relaxed and dozed off. Matthew Henry sees a picture here: people who give in to sinful desires are surrounded by spiritual enemies, and the safer they feel, the greater their danger.

At midnight Samson got up and tore the city gates out of the ground, posts, bar and all. He carried them to a hilltop facing toward Hebron. This was probably a hill near Gaza that looks toward the Hebron hills. Matthew Henry hopes Samson's conscience woke him with sorrow over his sin. The feat showed the strength God had given him and made fun of the Philistines. God was using Samson in spite of his sin, not because of it.

Later Samson fell in love with Delilah, who lived in the Valley of Sorek. Commentators suspect this was a sinful relationship and not a marriage. It is not certain whether she was an Israelite or a Philistine. This is the third time a woman pulls Samson into danger, and this time it ruins him.

The five Philistine rulers came to Delilah. They thought Samson's strength came from a charm or secret, and they wanted to tie him up and humble him. Each offered her 1,100 pieces of silver, a huge sum. Matthew Henry compares this to Jesus being betrayed by a friend for money.
Delilah asked Samson straight out what made him so strong and how he could be tied up. She acted as if she were only curious. She worked on him when he was in a soft, chatty mood.

Samson gave her a false answer: seven fresh bowstrings, probably made from animal sinew. Adam Clarke thinks Samson was playing along with the Philistine idea of a magic charm. Fresh strings and the number seven sound like the stuff of a spell.

The rulers brought the bowstrings, and Delilah tied Samson up, maybe as if it were a game. Men hid in an inner room. When she shouted that the Philistines were there, he snapped the strings like yarn touched by fire. The hidden men probably never came out, so his secret stayed safe.

Delilah complained that he had lied to her, and he gave a second false answer: brand-new ropes. Again he broke them like thread. Matthew Henry wonders why Samson stayed. He could see she wanted to harm him, yet he kept putting his head back in her lap. His feelings for her clouded his thinking.

The third time, Samson told her to weave his seven braids into the cloth on her loom and pin it tight. The Hebrew text here is shortened, and an old Greek translation fills in the missing words. When he woke, he pulled the whole loom away. This answer came closer to the truth. By letting his hair be handled, Samson was already toying with the gift God had given him. These attempts may have been days apart.

Delilah used his love as a weapon: how could he say he loved her if he kept secrets? Matthew Henry notes a true point inside her trick: real love means our heart is with someone, not just our words. But she was the one whose heart was false, and she accused him of what she herself was doing.

She nagged him every day until he was sick of living. At last he told her everything. He was a Nazirite, a person set apart to God by a vow, and no razor had ever touched his head. His strength was never really in his hair. It came from his special bond with God, and his long hair was the sign of that bond. Matthew Henry says God left him to his own folly because he kept giving in to lust.

Delilah could tell he had finally told the truth, so she called the rulers back. They came with the money in their hands. Matthew Henry notes she made sure of her pay first. One of the bravest men alive was being sold like a sheep.

Delilah lulled Samson to sleep on her lap, and a man shaved off his seven braids. His strength left him. Matthew Henry sees how Satan works: he lulls people into feeling safe, then robs them. When we sleep, our spiritual enemies do not. The hair was not magic. It was the sign of Samson's promise to God.

Samson woke up and thought he would shake free as before. But he did not know the LORD had left him. Samson had said his strength would go, but the writer says the LORD had gone, and that is the real point. Matthew Henry warns that many people lose the sense of God's presence and do not even notice.

The Philistines grabbed him, gouged out his eyes, and took him to Gaza in bronze chains. There he had to grind grain, the lowest kind of slave work. His eyes had led him into sin, and now his punishment began there. He was put to work in the very city where he had once shown off his strength.

His hair began to grow back. Commentators see this as a sign that Samson had turned back to God in sorrow, and that God's favor was returning. One old writer said, "His hair grew together with his repentance, and his strength with his hairs." His eyes, though, were never restored. Forgiveness does not always undo the results of sin in this life.

The Philistines held a big feast for their god Dagon, an idol pictured as part man, part fish. They praised Dagon for handing Samson to them, even though they had paid Delilah to betray him. Samson's sin gave glory to a false god. Matthew Henry adds that we have far more reason to thank the true God for every good thing.

Drunk and happy, the crowd called for Samson to entertain them. He was probably mocked and pushed around, and perhaps made to show off his strength. Matthew Henry says mocking God's servants, even when their own folly brought them low, fills up a people's guilt quickly. They placed him between the pillars.

Samson asked the boy leading him to let him feel the pillars so he could lean on them. The building was packed, with all the rulers inside and about three thousand people on the roof. The building likely rested its weight on two central pillars standing close together. If those gave way, the whole thing would fall.

Samson prayed: "Remember me, and strengthen me just once more." It is the first time we see him pray in this chapter. The strength he lost by sin, he now seeks by prayer, like a man truly sorry for his sin. Commentators think it may have been a silent prayer, and God answered it. It is this faith that puts Samson among the heroes of faith in Hebrews 11:32. His words also show how deeply he felt the loss of his eyes.

Samson braced against the two middle pillars and said, "Let me die with the Philistines." He pushed, and the temple fell on the rulers and the crowd. He killed more in his death than in his life. The traditional view is that this was not self-murder. He was a leader of Israel fighting its enemies, and he aimed at their defeat, not his own death. Matthew Henry says the building fell by God's mighty power, not by Samson's own muscles.

differ.view: Some say it was a kind of suicide, even though his goal was to kill Israel's enemies. The Bible does not praise that part of his act, and Samson is a tragic hero of faith.

notes.meaning: The disaster shocked the Philistines so badly that Samson's family could safely come and take his body home. They buried him in his father Manoah's tomb. The story ends by repeating that he judged, or led, Israel for twenty years. His life was marred by his passions, yet Hebrews 11:32 still counts him among those who trusted God.
